learn.hook: Every whole number above 1 is built from prime 'bricks' — and there is only ONE way to build it!
points: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the primes.
Find it with a factor tree or by dividing again and again by the smallest prime that fits.
A number ends in 0 only if both 2 and 5 are among its prime factors. So 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ can never end in 0.

example.q: Write 4620 as a product of primes.

learn.reallife: Computer security (like the lock on your UPI app) depends on how hard it is to find the prime factors of huge numbers.

games.title: Match each number to its prime factorisation
Prime brick check
items: Every composite number can be written as a product of primes.
That is exactly what the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says.
4ⁿ ends in the digit 0 for some natural number n.
4ⁿ = 2²ⁿ has only the prime 2. Ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5.
9 is a factor of 81 but 9 is not prime. The only prime factor of 81 is 3.
Writing 5 × 3 × 2 instead of 2 × 3 × 5 gives a different prime factorisation.
Uniqueness is 'apart from the order', so both are the same factorisation of 30.
10ⁿ ends in 0 for every natural number n.

quiz.q: Which is the prime factorisation of 360?
quiz.explain: 360 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Every factor must be prime.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a composite factor like 10 or 15, or miscounts the 2s

quiz.q: Riya's secret number is 2² × 3 × 5² × 7. What is the number?
quiz.explain: Multiply out the powers: 4 × 3 × 25 × 7 = 2100.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 instead of 5², or 2 instead of 2²

quiz.q: Why can 6ⁿ never end in the digit 0, for any natural number n?
options: Because its only prime factors are 2 and 3, so 5 never appears
quiz.explain: To end in 0 a number needs both 2 and 5 as prime factors. 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no 5, and by uniqueness it can never get one.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being even is enough to end in 0

quiz.q: How many different prime factors does 2310 have?
quiz.explain: 2310 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11, so it has 5 different primes.
quiz.mistake: Stops dividing too early and leaves a composite factor such as 77

quiz.q: For which value of b does bⁿ end in the digit 0 for every natural number n?
quiz.explain: 10 = 2 × 5, so 10ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 5ⁿ always has both 2 and 5. 12 has no 5, while 15 and 25 have no 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks having just one of the primes 2 or 5 is enough

quiz.q: Which is the prime factorisation of 156?
quiz.mistake: Leaves a composite factor like 26 or 39 in the answer

quiz.q: Arjun's number is 2⁴ × 5³. What is it?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the base by the power (2 × 4, 5 × 3) instead of repeated multiplication

quiz.q: The theorem says the prime factorisation is 'unique'. What does unique mean here?
options: Only prime numbers can be factorised
The primes must be written from largest to smallest
Every number has a different number of factors
There is only one set of primes, apart from the order they are written in
quiz.explain: However you split a number, you always end with the same primes the same number of times; only the order may change.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'unique' with a fixed writing order

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'Why is 2 × 2 × 3 the only way to break 12 into primes? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Same primes every time, only the order changes. My prime bricks are sorted!
teach.nudge: But what if I write the primes in a different order — is that a new factorisation?

topics.title: HCF and LCM using prime factors

learn.hook: Two bells, three buses or a box of laddoos — HCF and LCM tell you when things meet and how to share fairly!
points: Write each number as a product of primes first.
HCF = product of the SMALLEST power of each prime that is common to all the numbers.
LCM = product of the GREATEST power of every prime that appears in any of the numbers.
For two positive integers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. This rule does not work in general for three numbers.
The HCF always divides the LCM.

example.q: Find the HCF and LCM of 84 and 120, and check the product rule.
steps: Common primes with smallest powers: 2² and 3, so HCF = 12
All primes with greatest powers: 2³, 3, 5, 7, so LCM = 8 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 840

learn.reallife: Traffic lights that turn green together, school bells, or packing sweets into equal boxes for Diwali gifts all use HCF and LCM.

items.text: If HCF = 5 and LCM = 60 for two numbers, their product = ___

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 36 and 60?
quiz.explain: 36 = 2² × 3² and 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. Common primes with smallest powers: 2² × 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Picks a smaller common factor, or gives the LCM

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 36 and 60?
quiz.explain: Take every prime with its greatest power: 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.
quiz.mistake: Just multiplies the two numbers (36 × 60 = 2160)

quiz.q: The HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 270. One number is 45. What is the other?
quiz.explain: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers, so the other number = 9 × 270 ÷ 45 = 54.
quiz.mistake: Divides LCM by the number without using the HCF (270 ÷ 45 = 6) or guesses a multiple of 9

quiz.q: If HCF(a, b) = 1, then LCM(a, b) is equal to…
quiz.explain: HCF × LCM = a × b. With HCF = 1, LCM = a × b.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the LCM must also be 1

quiz.q: Can two numbers have HCF 16 and LCM 380?
options: Yes, any HCF and LCM are possible
No, because 380 is not a prime
quiz.explain: The HCF must always divide the LCM. 380 ÷ 16 = 23.75, not a whole number, so this is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the HCF always divides the LCM

quiz.q: Three temple bells ring every 12, 15 and 20 minutes. They ring together at 8:00 AM. When will they next ring together?
quiz.explain: They meet after LCM(12, 15, 20) = 60 minutes, which is 9:00 AM.
quiz.mistake: Adds the gaps (12 + 15 + 20 = 47 min) or uses the largest gap only

quiz.q: Meena has 96 laddoos and 120 barfis. She packs them in boxes, one kind per box, with the same number in every box and as many as possible per box. How many sweets go in each box?
quiz.explain: The biggest number that divides both 96 and 120 is HCF(96, 120) = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM (480) when the problem asks for the greatest equal share

quiz.q: For the three numbers 4, 6 and 8, what is HCF × LCM?
quiz.explain: HCF(4, 6, 8) = 2 and LCM = 24, so HCF × LCM = 48. That is NOT 4 × 6 × 8 = 192, so the product rule is only for two numbers.
quiz.mistake: Assumes HCF × LCM = product of the numbers also works for three numbers

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'How do I find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using primes?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Smallest common powers for HCF, biggest powers for LCM. I can share my laddoos now!
teach.nudge: Which powers do I pick for the HCF and which for the LCM — the smaller or the bigger ones?

learn.hook: √2 has been hiding as a 'fake fraction' for 2500 years — today you catch it with a proof!
points: A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: √2, √3, √5, π.
We prove irrationality by contradiction: assume the number is rational, then reach something impossible.
Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
Proof idea for √2: assume √2 = a/b with a, b co-prime. Squaring gives a² = 2b², so 2 divides a. Put a = 2c: then b² = 2c², so 2 divides b too — but a and b had no common factor. Contradiction!
Rational + irrational is irrational, and a non-zero rational × irrational is irrational. But two irrationals can add or multiply to a rational (√2 × √2 = 2).

example.q: Show that 5 + 3√2 is irrational, given that √2 is irrational.
steps: Assume 5 + 3√2 = r, where r is rational
(r − 5)/3 is rational, because rationals are closed under subtraction and division by a non-zero number
That would make √2 rational — a contradiction

learn.reallife: Engineers use √2 for the diagonal of a square tile and π for round wheels — their decimals never end or repeat, so measurements are always rounded.

games.title: Put the proof that √5 is irrational in order
items: Assume √5 = a/b, where a and b are co-prime integers
So 5 divides a²; hence 5 divides a. Write a = 5c
Then 25c² = 5b², so b² = 5c² and 5 divides b
5 divides both a and b, which contradicts co-prime, so √5 is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these is irrational?
quiz.explain: √12 = 2√3 and √3 is irrational. √16 = 4, 0.75 = 3/4 and 22/7 are all fractions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 22/7 is irrational because it is close to π

quiz.q: To prove √3 is irrational we assume √3 = a/b with a, b co-prime. What do we get after squaring and rearranging?
quiz.explain: Squaring gives 3 = a²/b², so a² = 3b².
quiz.mistake: Squares only one side, or swaps a and b

quiz.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational, why do we start by taking a and b co-prime?
options: Because a and b must both be prime
So that a must be even
So that a and b are both odd
So that finding a common factor 2 gives a contradiction
quiz.explain: Any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms. If we then show 2 divides both a and b, that clashes with 'no common factor'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'co-prime' with 'both numbers are prime'

quiz.q: Which of these is rational?
quiz.explain: (3 + √5) − √5 = 3, which is rational. The others stay irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any expression containing a square root must be irrational

quiz.q: Why is 6 + √2 irrational?
options: Because a rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational
Because every sum of numbers is irrational
quiz.explain: If 6 + √2 were rational, then √2 = (6 + √2) − 6 would be rational too — impossible.
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason that has nothing to do with rational/irrational

quiz.q: What is √3 × √12?
quiz.explain: √3 × √12 = √36 = 6. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational number.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root, or forgets to take the square root of 36

quiz.q: Kabir says, 'Both factors are irrational, so √5 × √5 must be irrational.' Is he right?
options: Yes, irrational × irrational is always irrational
quiz.explain: √5 × √5 = 5. The product of two irrationals can be rational.
quiz.mistake: Overgeneralises: thinks irrationals always multiply to irrationals

quiz.q: Which statement is ALWAYS true?
options: The sum of two irrational numbers is irrational
The product of two irrational numbers is irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is irrational
The square root of every whole number is irrational
quiz.explain: If q × x = r with q, r rational and q ≠ 0, then x = r/q is rational, a contradiction. The others fail: √2 + (−√2) = 0, √2 × √2 = 2, √9 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Treats a rule that works sometimes as one that always works

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'How can you be SURE √2 is not a fraction? Prove it to me!'
teach.praise: Wow, a proof by contradiction! √2 can't hide behind a fraction any more. Tweet!
teach.nudge: What do we pretend first, and what impossible thing do we reach at the end?
